sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent PairFormer-based approaches demonstrate strong capabilities in biomolecular binder design, including RFdiffusion3, BoltzDesign1, BoltzGen, and PPIFlow ( Butcher et al., 2025 ; Cho et al., 2025 ; Stark et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . However, existing methods often use all-atom representations for modality-specific binder design, such as protein and peptide design. In parallel, geometric latent diffusion models pursue unified binder design by representing molecular blocks from different modalities in a shared latent space. Building on this formulation, UniMoMo and AnewOmni support binder design across different molecular classes ( Kong et al., 2025 ; Kong et al., 2026 ) . These advances motivate us to generalize pretrained all-atom representations to unified binder design through parameter-efficient representation fusion. Existing methods, including IP-Adapter ( Ye et al., 2023 ) , LLM4GEN ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , and EnzyAdapter ( Song et al., 2025 ) , incorporate pretrained representations into generative models through lightweight adaptation. However, these methods focus on feature-level conditioning and do not explicitly address how pairwise structural information can be transferred to guide geometric interactions during denoising. The challenge is therefore to integrate pretrained information about both molecular components and their interactions into an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model. To address these challenges, we introduce PairFuse , a parameter-efficient method for extending pretrained all-atom representations to unified binder design through representation fusion. We instantiate PairFuse on AnewOmni ( Kong et al., 2026 ) , an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model, using single and pair representations extracted from a pretrained BoltzGen PairFormer ( Stark et al., 2025 ) . Our lightweight layerwise adapters fuse these representations into the geometric diffusion denoiser through two mechanisms. First, cross-attention enriches the diffusion model’s invariant molecular block features with pretrained structural information. Second, additive attention biases incorporate pretrained pairwise relationships into the Transformer’s attention to guide denoising. This design preserves the original equivariant vector operations while keeping both pretrained models frozen and training only the adapters. A key consideration in representation fusion for geometric latent diffusion is preserving rotational equivariance when incorporating pretrained structural information into native geometric attention. The geometric denoiser processes three-dimensional molecular structures, and its coordinate predictions transform consistently under rotations ( Fuchs et al., 2020 ; Satorras et al., 2021 ; Jing et al., 2021 ; Kong et al., 2024a ) . PairFuse incorporates pretrained all-atom representations into rotation-invariant block features and native geometric attention without modifying the equivariant vector operations. We prove that the augmented denoiser preserves rotational equivariance under rotation-invariant transferred representations. This guarantee holds for arbitrary learned adapter parameters, establishing the geometric compatibility of PairFuse. We evaluate PairFuse on antibody, peptide, and small-molecule binder-design benchmarks: RAbD ( Adolf-Bryfogle et al., 2018 ) , LNR ( Tsaban et al., 2022 ) , and CrossDocked2020 ( Francoeur et al., 2020 ) . PairFuse improves structural accuracy and interface quality on antibody and peptide design and achieves competitive performance on small-molecule design. These results support the effectiveness of parameter-efficient representation fusion for unified binder design.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: Our contributions are three-fold. • Pretrained All-Atom Representation Fusion. We propose PairFuse, a parameter-efficient method that extends the use of pretrained all-atom representations to unified binder design. Our layerwise adapters integrate pretrained single and pair representations into the evolving invariant block features and native geometric attention of a geometric latent diffusion model. We freeze both pretrained models and retain the original latent space, sampling procedure, and all-atom decoder ( Section 3 ). • Theoretical Analysis. We prove that PairFuse preserves rotational equivariance under rotation-invariant transferred representations ( Theorem 3.1 ). We further characterize the expressivity of pairwise attention fusion. Under a stated rank condition, direct attention fusion expresses attention patterns that scalar-feature-only fusion cannot reproduce through fixed-width native query–key projections ( Theorem 3.2 ). • Empirical Evaluation. We evaluate PairFuse across antibody, peptide, and small-molecule binder design using shared fusion checkpoints. PairFuse improves structural accuracy and interface quality on antibody and peptide benchmarks and achieves favorable results on small-molecule design ( Section 4.2 ). We further investigate the contributions of single and pair representations and pairwise attention fusion through ablation studies ( Appendix E ). We report experimental details, statistical analyses, and computational efficiency ( Appendix D ).

sections.heading: 2 Preliminaries
sections.text: We introduce the unified biomolecular design setting, geometric latent diffusion, the Equivariant Pretrained Transformer (EPT), and pretrained all-atom representations.

sections.heading: Unified Binder Design and Latent Representation.
sections.text: Unified geometric latent diffusion models, such as UniMoMo and AnewOmni ( Kong et al., 2025 ; Kong et al., 2026 ) , represent different molecular classes in a shared latent space. Let c c denote the design condition, including the target, design region, binder type, and prescribed constraints. We seek to generate a binder x x from the conditional distribution p θ ​ ( x ∣ c ) p_{\theta}(x\mid c) . Specifically, each molecular block (e.g., an amino acid residue in a peptide or a molecular fragment in a small-molecule ligand) is represented by an invariant feature and a three-dimensional coordinate, yielding z = ( h , q ) , h ∈ ℝ n × d , q ∈ ℝ n × 3 , \displaystyle z=(h,q),\qquad h\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d},\quad q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 3}, for n n molecular blocks. A pretrained all-atom decoder D D reconstructs the binder from the generated latent blocks and design condition c c .

sections.heading: Pretrained All-Atom Representations.
sections.text: PairFormer-based all-atom binder-design models, such as RFdiffusion3 and BoltzGen ( Butcher et al., 2025 ; Stark et al., 2025 ) , learn single and pair representations that capture token-level structural information and pairwise interactions. Given the visible design condition c c , we denote these pretrained representations by r ⁡ ( c ) = ( S , P ) r(c)=(S,P) , where S S contains token-level single representations and P P contains pair representations encoding learned relations between token pairs. Figure 1 : Overview of PairFuse. A frozen BoltzGen PairFormer extracts pretrained single and pair representations, while AnewOmni provides the geometric latent diffusion model. sections.heading: 3 Pretrained All-Atom Representation Fusion
sections.text: We introduce PairFuse , a parameter-efficient method that integrates pretrained all-atom representations into geometric latent diffusion through layerwise fusion. We instantiate PairFuse on AnewOmni ( Kong et al., 2026 ) , using single and pair representations extracted from a pretrained BoltzGen PairFormer ( Stark et al., 2025 ) . As illustrated in Figure 1 , our layerwise adapters integrate these representations into the evolving invariant scalar features and native geometric attention logits of EPT. We freeze both pretrained models and train only the adapters. We first introduce the layerwise representation fusion mechanism ( Section 3.1 ), then establish its geometric compatibility ( Section 3.2 ), and finally present the training and inference procedures ( Section 3.3 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Layerwise All-Atom Representation Fusion
sections.text: PairFuse integrates pretrained PairFormer representations into two components of each EPT layer: invariant scalar features and native attention logits. We introduce scalar-feature fusion and pairwise attention fusion to incorporate pretrained structural information into these components.

sections.heading: 3.3 Training and Inference
sections.text: We freeze the BoltzGen trunk and the pretrained AnewOmni parameters θ \theta and optimize only the fusion parameters ϕ \phi . Gradients propagate through the frozen denoiser to the adapters. Let ϵ h \epsilon_{h} and ϵ q \epsilon_{q} denote the noise added to the generated block features and coordinates, respectively. We retain the native noise-prediction objective: ℒ fusion ​ ( ϕ ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ λ n G ​ ‖ ϵ aug , h − ϵ h ‖ F 2 + 1 n G ​ ‖ ϵ aug , q − ϵ q ‖ F 2 ] , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fusion}}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\lambda}{n_{G}}\left\|\epsilon_{\mathrm{aug},h}-\epsilon_{h}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{1}{n_{G}}\left\|\epsilon_{\mathrm{aug},q}-\epsilon_{q}\right\|_{F}^{2}\right], (3.10) where n G n_{G} is the number of generated blocks and λ \lambda weights the latent-feature loss. Predictions and noise targets are restricted to generated blocks. Context rows of z t z_{t} remain fixed, although their internal EPT features participate in fusion. No additional structural supervision is introduced. At inference time, the learned fusion adapters are applied at each EPT layer using the same operations as during training. The PairFormer representations are cached and reused throughout reverse diffusion. The native sampling procedure and pretrained all-atom decoder remain unchanged.

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Studies
sections.text: We evaluate PairFuse on antibody, peptide, and small-molecule binder design. Our goal is to assess whether pretrained all-atom representations can improve an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model through parameter-efficient representation fusion. We compare PairFuse against the original AnewOmni checkpoint and three adapted representation-fusion baselines. Additional experimental details are provided in Appendix D .

sections.heading: Task and Benchmark.
sections.text: We evaluate HCDR3 design on RAbD ( Adolf-Bryfogle et al., 2018 ) , peptide design on LNR ( Tsaban et al., 2022 ) , and small-molecule design on CrossDocked2020 ( Francoeur et al., 2020 ) . The fixed evaluation sets contain 60 RAbD targets, 93 LNR targets, and a 100-target subset of CrossDocked2020, respectively.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare against AnewOmni ( Kong et al., 2026 ) , LLM4GEN ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , EnzyAdapter ( Song et al., 2025 ) , and IP-Adapter ( Ye et al., 2023 ) . AnewOmni uses its original pretrained checkpoint without additional training. LLM4GEN and EnzyAdapter adapt the respective representation-fusion mechanisms to the AnewOmni backbone. LLM4GEN applies a single cross-attention module to update native conditioning before the unchanged denoiser. EnzyAdapter uses layerwise cross-attention, concatenation, and projection modules. IP-Adapter applies decoupled cross-attention at each EPT layer, using native queries to attend separately to projected PairFormer single representations. The donor scalar output is added before the shared frozen output projection. All fusion baselines are trained on the common biomolecular task. All trained representation-fusion methods are matched in trainable parameter count (approximately 4.03 million, with a maximum relative difference below 0.1%), with details reported in Table 5 .

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: Following AnewOmni ( Kong et al., 2026 ) , we evaluate structural accuracy and amino-acid recovery for antibody and peptide design. We additionally assess interface quality through local-interface adaptations of DockQ and native-contact recall ( Basu and Wallner, 2016 ) , together with a backbone interface score based on lDDT ( Mariani et al., 2013 ) . For small-molecule design, we report Vina score and Vina min ( Trott and Olson, 2010 ) , High Affinity ( Guan et al., 2023 ) , QED ( Bickerton et al., 2012 ) , and Atom-type MAE ( Lin et al., 2024 ) . Additional metrics, including steric clashes, interface RMSD, and Lipinski rule compliance ( Lipinski et al., 1997 ) , are reported in the appendix. We use 30 fixed generation attempts per target. Native metrics pool finite candidate scores within each run, whereas interface and supplementary structural metrics first average finite candidates within each target and then weight targets equally. We select one checkpoint per trained run by minimizing the combined native validation loss on a 614-record validation set, weighting each modality by its number of generated blocks. The selected checkpoint is shared across all three modalities. Metric definitions and evaluation procedures are provided in Section D.5 . PairFormer-representation construction and training details are provided in Sections D.2 and D.3 .

sections.heading: Antibody Design.
sections.text: On RAbD, PairFuse achieves the lowest mean complex RMSD and the highest mean DockQ and native-contact recall. Relative to AnewOmni, complex RMSD decreases from 2.5563 to 2.3748 Å, DockQ increases from 0.6853 to 0.7019, and native-contact recall improves from 50.9592% to 52.4309%. sections.heading: Overall Results.
sections.text: Across antibody and peptide design, PairFuse consistently achieves the lowest mean complex RMSD and the highest mean scores on all three interface-quality metrics. For small-molecule design, PairFuse achieves favorable mean docking scores with broadly comparable performance on other chemical-quality metrics. These results support the effectiveness of parameter-efficient fusion of pretrained all-atom representations for unified binder design. Detailed implementation settings, including computational resources, training hyperparameters, checkpoint selection, and inference, are provided in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 4.3 Ablation Studies and Implementation Details
sections.text: We examine whether transferring pretrained pair representations directly into native attention improves interface quality beyond scalar-feature fusion. We compare Full PairFuse with two controls. Scalar Fusion retains scalar-feature fusion, including its pair conditioning, but removes the additive conditioning of native attention logits. Scalar Fusion + + Cross-Attention Bias additionally retains the single-conditioned term in ( 3.3 ), omitting only the direct pair contribution. All variants receive the same pretrained representations ( S , P ) (S,P) and use the same frozen backbone, training data, twenty-hour training budget, and validation-based checkpoint-selection rule. We evaluate training seed 42 on 93 peptide and 60 antibody targets with 30 generation attempts per target, averaging candidate scores within each target before weighting targets equally. Table 4 shows that Full PairFuse achieves higher scores on all three interface metrics and lower complex RMSD than both controls in both tasks. Compared with Scalar Fusion + + Cross-Attention Bias (abbreviated as Scalar Fusion + + Bias in the table), it achieves DockQ of 0.4397 versus 0.4329, contact recall of 34.2175% versus 33.5094%, and backbone interface lDDT of 0.4309 versus 0.4233 on peptide design. The corresponding antibody scores are 0.7024 versus 0.6849, 52.4474% versus 50.8340%, and 0.7017 versus 0.6848, respectively. Complex RMSD decreases from 8.3991 to 8.2543 Å on peptide design and from 2.5625 to 2.3704 Å on antibody design. For the evaluated checkpoints, all six paired improvements in the three interface metrics pooled across peptide and antibody targets have pointwise 95% target-bootstrap confidence intervals above zero. These results support an additional benefit of transferring pretrained pair representations directly into native attention beyond their use in scalar-feature fusion. sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduce PairFuse , a parameter-efficient framework for extending pretrained all-atom representations to unified binder design. PairFuse integrates pretrained PairFormer single and pair representations into the evolving invariant block features and native geometric attention of a geometric latent diffusion model, while keeping both pretrained models frozen. Theoretically, we prove that PairFuse preserves rotational equivariance and characterize the additional expressivity of pairwise attention fusion under a stated rank condition ( Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 ). Experimentally, PairFuse achieves the lowest mean complex RMSD and the highest mean interface-quality scores on antibody and peptide benchmarks. For small-molecule design, it achieves favorable docking and atom-type metrics, with mixed results on other chemical-quality metrics ( Section 4.2 ). A limitation is that unknown generated molecular structures, particularly small-molecule ligands, lack direct PairFormer token correspondences, which may affect representation-transfer effectiveness. Future work will explore representation-fusion mechanisms that better accommodate unknown molecular structures and additional pretrained all-atom models.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Work
sections.text: Our approach connects unified biomolecular generation with pretrained all-atom structural representations. We review related work in molecular design, equivariant geometric modeling, and lightweight adaptation to place this connection in context.

sections.heading: Protein and Peptide Design.
sections.text: Deep generative models have been applied to protein sequence design, structure generation, and binder optimization. ProteinMPNN performs sequence design conditioned on protein backbones ( Dauparas et al., 2022 ) . RFdiffusion, Chroma, and FrameDiff generate protein structures through geometric diffusion or related generative processes ( Watson et al., 2023 ; Ingraham et al., 2023 ; Yim et al., 2023 ) . DiffAb studies antigen-conditioned antibody sequence–structure design ( Luo et al., 2022 ) . PepGLAD and PepFlow address full-atom peptide generation through geometric latent diffusion and multimodal flow matching ( Kong et al., 2024b ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Structure predictors have also been incorporated into peptide docking and binder optimization pipelines ( Tsaban et al., 2022 ; Pacesa et al., 2025 ) . These advances motivate the use of pretrained structural representations for unified binder design. PairFuse integrates such representations into a geometric latent diffusion model that generates binders.

sections.heading: Unified Biomolecular Generation.
sections.text: Recent work seeks broader generative interfaces across heterogeneous molecular classes. UniMoMo and AnewOmni represent different molecular entities through shared block-level latent states ( Kong et al., 2025 ; Kong et al., 2026 ) . PocketXMol adopts atom-level representations for molecular interaction modeling, while ODesign studies broad all-atom biomolecular interaction design ( Peng et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . La-Proteina combines explicit backbone geometry with latent representations of sequence and side-chain structure ( Geffner et al., 2025 ) . Proteina-Complexa extends atomistic generative modeling to protein binder design with large-scale pretraining and test-time computation ( Didi et al., 2026 ) . PairFuse connects these approaches by incorporating pretrained all-atom representations into the shared latent space of AnewOmni through layerwise fusion.

sections.heading: All-Atom Biomolecular Models.
sections.text: Recent all-atom biomolecular models maintain token-level and pairwise representations before structure prediction or generation. AlphaFold introduced learned representations for high-accuracy protein structure prediction ( Jumper et al., 2021 ) . RoseTTAFold All-Atom and AlphaFold 3 extend structural modeling across proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, and other molecular entities ( Krishna et al., 2024 ; Abramson et al., 2024 ) . Boltz-2 further combines biomolecular structure modeling with binding-affinity prediction ( Passaro et al., 2025 ) . Recent generative models such as RFdiffusion3 and BoltzGen perform all-atom biomolecular generation ( Butcher et al., 2025 ; Stark et al., 2025 ) . We extract single and pair representations from the frozen BoltzGen PairFormer and integrate them into the AnewOmni denoiser. These representations provide structural information about individual molecular blocks and their interactions.

sections.heading: Equivariant Geometric Models.
sections.text: Geometric neural networks incorporate rotational and translational symmetry through equivariant attention, message passing, and vector-valued representations ( Fuchs et al., 2020 ; Satorras et al., 2021 ; Jing et al., 2021 ) . The Generalist Equivariant Transformer extends these ideas to molecular interaction learning across heterogeneous chemical systems ( Kong et al., 2024a ) . AnewOmni similarly combines invariant latent features with equivariant three-dimensional coordinates ( Kong et al., 2026 ) . PairFuse integrates all-atom representations into invariant scalar features and pairwise attention while retaining the native equivariant vector operations. We establish that this layerwise fusion preserves rotational equivariance under rotation-invariant transferred representations.

sections.heading: Lightweight Model Adaptation.
sections.text: Parameter-efficient adaptation has been studied through trainable bottleneck adapters and low-rank weight updates ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) . Frozen pretrained models have also been connected through compact learned interfaces in multimodal systems such as Flamingo and BLIP-2 ( Alayrac et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ) . For diffusion models, ControlNet and T2I-Adapter inject additional structural conditions into pretrained generators ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Mou et al., 2024 ) , while IP-Adapter transfers external representations through cross-attention ( Ye et al., 2023 ) . We extend this approach to unified biomolecular binder design by connecting a pretrained all-atom model with a geometric latent diffusion model. Lightweight adapters transfer PairFormer representations through layerwise scalar residuals and attention biases, allowing both pretrained backbones to remain frozen.

sections.heading: Appendix D Experimental Details
sections.text: Our implementation combines frozen pretrained representations with trainable layerwise fusion. We describe the construction of these representations, the training and model-selection procedure, and the inference and evaluation protocol used across the three design tasks.

sections.heading: D.1 Training, Validation, and Test Data
sections.text: We construct the adaptation data from the existing AnewOmni-format dataset partitions ( Kong et al., 2026 ) . Antibody examples are drawn from the SAbDab training partition ( Dunbar et al., 2014 ) , peptide examples from the ProtFrag and PepBench training partitions ( Kong et al., 2024b ) , and small-molecule examples from the PDBbind v2020 training partition ( Liu et al., 2015 ) . The validation set retains the corresponding source validation records: 400 antibody examples, 114 peptide examples, and 100 small-molecule examples, for a total of 614 records.

sections.heading: Training-Set Construction.
sections.text: Before sampling, we collect PDB identifiers from the source validation and test partitions across all three modalities, including the LNR peptide benchmark, and exclude matching entries from the training pools. Peptide preprocessing additionally excludes exact receptor–peptide sequence pairs present in its validation or LNR sets. We then freeze 10,000 logical training positions per modality, yielding 30,000 positions in total. Sampling uses eligible training records, with replacement when needed to reach the prescribed count. The peptide manifest contains 9,447 ProtFrag positions and 553 PepBench positions. For each antibody position, we randomly select one valid CDR and retain that identity throughout training; repeated complexes preferentially use previously unselected valid CDRs. The resulting training and validation manifests have no shared PDB identifiers, including across modalities, and remain fixed throughout optimization.

sections.heading: Validation and Test Evaluation.
sections.text: Validation data are used to select a single shared checkpoint for all three modalities according to the native denoising-loss criterion described below. Test evaluation uses the fixed benchmark collections of 60 RAbD antibody targets ( Adolf-Bryfogle et al., 2018 ) , 93 LNR peptide targets ( Tsaban et al., 2022 ; Kong et al., 2024b ) , and 100 CrossDocked2020 small-molecule targets ( Francoeur et al., 2020 ) , totaling 253 targets. These benchmark collections are assembled separately from the source training and validation partitions. Each model is evaluated with 30 generation attempts per target under the common inference protocol.

sections.heading: D.2 Construction of Pretrained Donor Representations
sections.text: We extract single and pair representations from the frozen BoltzGen PairFormer to provide structural information about individual molecular blocks and their interactions. The input contains the visible molecular context and the prescribed design positions, with the identity and coordinates of the generated region masked. The resulting representations are aligned with AnewOmni’s molecular blocks and reused throughout training and denoising.

sections.heading: Molecular Context and Design Positions.
sections.text: Visible protein residues retain their amino-acid identities and atomic coordinates. For peptide design, the prescribed peptide length determines the generated positions. For antibody design, the designated CDR determines these positions, while the retained framework and antigen provide structural context. Protein design positions are represented by backbone placeholders with zero coordinates and no structural visibility. Their residue identities are replaced by unknown tokens before feature extraction, so neither the reference binder sequence nor its geometry is available to the donor. Protein residues are tokenized at the residue level using the native all-atom design featurization. We use single-sequence inputs without external multiple-sequence alignments or retrieved structural templates; the visible context structure enters through the native structural-conditioning pathway.

sections.heading: Representation Extraction.
sections.text: The frozen donor processes each input with three recycling steps. We retain the single and pair representations from the final PairFormer output, before structure generation: S tok ∈ ℝ N tok × 384 , P tok ∈ ℝ N tok × N tok × 128 , S^{\mathrm{tok}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathrm{tok}}\times 384},\qquad P^{\mathrm{tok}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathrm{tok}}\times N_{\mathrm{tok}}\times 128}, (D.1) where N tok N_{\mathrm{tok}} denotes the number of donor tokens. These features encode token-level structural information and pairwise relationships without requiring a sampled BoltzGen structure. Feature extraction is performed in evaluation mode without gradient computation, using bfloat16 mixed precision. Single and pair representations are retained in float32 and bfloat16, respectively, and projected by the trainable fusion encoders during adaptation.

sections.heading: Correspondence with Molecular Blocks.
sections.text: We align donor tokens with AnewOmni blocks using chain identifiers and residue correspondence. Blocks derived from the same protein residue share the corresponding donor token, and chain discontinuities are preserved. Let π ⁡ ( i ) \pi(i) denote the donor token associated with block i i , and let m i ∈ { 0 , 1 } m_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether this correspondence is available. The aligned features are S i = S π ⁡ ( i ) tok , P i ​ j = P π ⁡ ( i ) , π ⁡ ( j ) tok , S_{i}=S^{\mathrm{tok}}_{\pi(i)},\qquad P_{ij}=P^{\mathrm{tok}}_{\pi(i),\pi(j)}, (D.2) for covered blocks and block pairs. Unavailable features are excluded through the correspondence masks in the fusion equations. This alignment preserves the distinction between donor tokens and the block-level latent representation used by the geometric denoiser.

sections.heading: Small-Molecule Coverage.
sections.text: In de novo small-molecule design, the ligand identity and chemical graph are unknown. We therefore exclude the reference ligand from the donor input and set m i = 0 m_{i}=0 for generated ligand blocks. Nonprotein context without a validated token correspondence is treated similarly. The transferred representations describe the available protein context rather than the unknown ligand. Generated ligand blocks can nevertheless attend to covered context tokens through scalar cross-attention and the key-masked attention bias. They do not receive a directly aligned single representation or a pair representation requiring both endpoints to be covered. This restriction limits the ligand-specific information available for transfer and helps characterize the distinction between protein-binder and small-molecule design.

sections.heading: Reuse across Denoising Steps.
sections.text: The donor representations are computed once for each fixed molecular input and reused across training iterations and reverse-diffusion steps. They are independent of the current noisy latent state, whereas the fusion queries depend on the evolving EPT hidden features. The same masked representations are used when the native training condition sampler exposes additional generated-region information to AnewOmni. Donor features are not recomputed for each sampled condition. Both pretrained models remain frozen, and only the fusion parameters are optimized.

sections.heading: D.3 Training and Model Selection
sections.text: We train the fusion adapters on 10,000 fixed records per modality, with antibody CDR identities fixed throughout training. Both pretrained backbones remain frozen. Each PairFuse and baseline training run uses a twenty hour allocation on four NVIDIA A100, including initialization, training, and validation. We select the checkpoint with the lowest combined native validation total loss on the 614-record validation set. This criterion combines latent-feature and coordinate denoising losses using the native loss weighting and weights modality-level means by their numbers of generated blocks. Ties retain the earlier checkpoint. The selected checkpoint is shared across antibody, peptide, and small-molecule design. Table 5: Trainable parameter counts for the compared methods. sections.heading: D.4 Hyperparameters and Optimization
sections.text: The number of fusion layers is set to six, with one fusion module at each EPT layer. We use AdamW with a learning rate of 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , weight decay of 0.01, an effective batch size of 32, and gradient clipping at 1. The learning rate follows a 100-update warmup and a cosine schedule over the training allocation, with a minimum value of 20% of the initial learning rate. PairFuse uses training seeds 20261007, 42, and 123, with checkpoints selected at updates 2,838, 2,732, and 2,500, respectively. IP-Adapter and EnzyAdapter use training seeds 1, 123, and 42. LLM4GEN uses three training seeds: 1, 123123, and 42. The pathway controls use training seed 42. Training uses modality-specific microbatches under the native batch-cost limit.

sections.heading: D.5 Inference and Evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate 60 RAbD targets, 93 LNR targets, and 100 CrossDocked2020 targets. Each model receives 30 generation attempts per target, using 100 diffusion steps, and batch size 10. For antibody and peptide design, we report structural RMSD, amino-acid recovery, steric clashes, Rosetta energies, and interface quality. Interface metrics comprise local-interface DockQ, interface RMSD, native contact recall, and backbone interface lDDT. Native metrics pool finite candidates within each run; interface metrics average candidates within each target and then weight targets equally. For small-molecule design, we report Vina scores, QED, normalized synthetic accessibility, and Lipinski rule compliance, pooling candidate scores. The original structural, energy, and chemical metrics follow the definitions used in AnewOmni ( Kong et al., 2026 ) . For the four interface metrics, residues are matched by their benchmark identities and design-block correspondence. Native-contact recall is the percentage of reference interfacial residue pairs with a heavy-atom distance below 5 Å that are recovered in the generated complex. Interface RMSD measures backbone deviation after superposing the native interface residues, defined by a 10 Å interchain distance threshold. DockQ combines native-contact recovery, interface RMSD, and receptor-aligned binder RMSD using the standard DockQ normalization. Backbone interface lDDT averages distance-recovery fractions at 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 Å tolerances over reference target–binder backbone-atom pairs within 15 Å. Missing generated atoms count as unrecovered pairs.

sections.text: We examine how single and pair representations contribute to generation quality and quantify the computational overhead of layerwise fusion. The efficiency analysis compares inference runtime and memory usage with the pretrained baseline.

sections.heading: Effect of Single Representations.
sections.text: Adding single representations to pair-only fusion improves all five displayed metrics on both antibody and peptide benchmarks, including all three interface-quality metrics. For antibodies, the gains extend from complex RMSD and DockQ to Rosetta dG, which decreases from − 2.2303 -2.2303 to − 8.1333 -8.1333 REU. For peptides, interface RMSD decreases from 3.0615 to 2.9919 Å and contact recall increases from 33.4552% to 34.1400%, while pair-only fusion gives the lower intra-region clash rate (0.8165% versus 0.8982%). These results support using both representations to improve protein-binder geometry and interface recovery. For ligand design, pair-only fusion yields a higher QED than joint fusion (0.5801 versus 0.5755). Together, these results show that single representations complement pair representations more consistently in antibody and peptide design, while introducing a trade-off between docking performance and chemical properties in ligand design.

Project page: jiale0402.github.io/all-atom-omni . † {}^{\dagger}\; Center for Foundation Models and Generative AI, Northwestern University Department of Computer Science, Northwestern University § {}^{\lx@sectionsign}\; Department of Statistics and Data Science, Northwestern University PairFormer-based all-atom models demonstrate strong capabilities in biomolecular binder design. However, existing methods often use all-atom representations for modality-specific binder design, such as protein and peptide design. In contrast, recent geometric latent diffusion models pursue unified binder design by representing molecular blocks from different modalities in a shared latent space. These complementary strengths motivate us to investigate how to generalize the use of pretrained all-atom representations to unified binder design. We introduce PairFuse , a parameter-efficient method that enables this generalization through representation fusion. Specifically, we use lightweight layerwise adapters to integrate pretrained all-atom representations into an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model. Our adapters integrate pretrained all-atom representations through two mechanisms: enriching the diffusion model’s molecular block features and incorporating pairwise structural information into the geometric diffusion model’s denoiser. Theoretically, we prove that the augmented denoiser preserves geometry and pairwise attention fusion provides additional attention expressivity beyond feature-only fusion. Experimentally, across antibody, peptide, and small molecule binder-design benchmarks, PairFuse achieves stronger performance than the pretrained diffusion model and existing representation-fusion baselines. 1 Introduction Recent PairFormer-based approaches demonstrate strong capabilities in biomolecular binder design, including RFdiffusion3, BoltzDesign1, BoltzGen, and PPIFlow ( Butcher et al., 2025 ; Cho et al., 2025 ; Stark et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . However, existing methods often use all-atom representations for modality-specific binder design, such as protein and peptide design. In parallel, geometric latent diffusion models pursue unified binder design by representing molecular blocks from different modalities in a shared latent space. Building on this formulation, UniMoMo and AnewOmni support binder design across different molecular classes ( Kong et al., 2025 ; Kong et al., 2026 ) . These advances motivate us to generalize pretrained all-atom representations to unified binder design through parameter-efficient representation fusion. Existing methods, including IP-Adapter ( Ye et al., 2023 ) , LLM4GEN ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , and EnzyAdapter ( Song et al., 2025 ) , incorporate pretrained representations into generative models through lightweight adaptation. However, these methods focus on feature-level conditioning and do not explicitly address how pairwise structural information can be transferred to guide geometric interactions during denoising. The challenge is therefore to integrate pretrained information about both molecular components and their interactions into an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model. To address these challenges, we introduce PairFuse , a parameter-efficient method for extending pretrained all-atom representations to unified binder design through representation fusion. We instantiate PairFuse on AnewOmni ( Kong et al., 2026 ) , an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model, using single and pair representations extracted from a pretrained BoltzGen PairFormer ( Stark et al., 2025 ) . Our lightweight layerwise adapters fuse these representations into the geometric diffusion denoiser through two mechanisms. First, cross-attention enriches the diffusion model’s invariant molecular block features with pretrained structural information. Second, additive attention biases incorporate pretrained pairwise relationships into the Transformer’s attention to guide denoising. This design preserves the original equivariant vector operations while keeping both pretrained models frozen and training only the adapters. A key consideration in representation fusion for geometric latent diffusion is preserving rotational equivariance when incorporating pretrained structural information into native geometric attention. The geometric denoiser processes three-dimensional molecular structures, and its coordinate predictions transform consistently under rotations ( Fuchs et al., 2020 ; Satorras et al., 2021 ; Jing et al., 2021 ; Kong et al., 2024a ) . PairFuse incorporates pretrained all-atom representations into rotation-invariant block features and native geometric attention without modifying the equivariant vector operations. We prove that the augmented denoiser preserves rotational equivariance under rotation-invariant transferred representations. This guarantee holds for arbitrary learned adapter parameters, establishing the geometric compatibility of PairFuse. We evaluate PairFuse on antibody, peptide, and small-molecule binder-design benchmarks: RAbD ( Adolf-Bryfogle et al., 2018 ) , LNR ( Tsaban et al., 2022 ) , and CrossDocked2020 ( Francoeur et al., 2020 ) . PairFuse improves structural accuracy and interface quality on antibody and peptide design and achieves competitive performance on small-molecule design. These results support the effectiveness of parameter-efficient representation fusion for unified binder design. Contributions. Our contributions are three-fold. • Pretrained All-Atom Representation Fusion. We propose PairFuse, a parameter-efficient method that extends the use of pretrained all-atom representations to unified binder design. Our layerwise adapters integrate pretrained single and pair representations into the evolving invariant block features and native geometric attention of a geometric latent diffusion model. We freeze both pretrained models and retain the original latent space, sampling procedure, and all-atom decoder ( Section 3 ). • Theoretical Analysis. We prove that PairFuse preserves rotational equivariance under rotation-invariant transferred representations ( Theorem 3.1 ). We further characterize the expressivity of pairwise attention fusion. Under a stated rank condition, direct attention fusion expresses attention patterns that scalar-feature-only fusion cannot reproduce through fixed-width native query–key projections ( Theorem 3.2 ). • Empirical Evaluation. We evaluate PairFuse across antibody, peptide, and small-molecule binder design using shared fusion checkpoints. PairFuse improves structural accuracy and interface quality on antibody and peptide benchmarks and achieves favorable results on small-molecule design ( Section 4.2 ). We further investigate the contributions of single and pair representations and pairwise attention fusion through ablation studies ( Appendix E ). We report experimental details, statistical analyses, and computational efficiency ( Appendix D ). 2 Preliminaries We introduce the unified biomolecular design setting, geometric latent diffusion, the Equivariant Pretrained Transformer (EPT), and pretrained all-atom representations. Our goal is to assess whether pretrained all-atom representations can improve an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model through parameter-efficient representation fusion. We compare PairFuse against the original AnewOmni checkpoint and three adapted representation-fusion baselines. Additional experimental details are provided in Appendix D . 4.1 Experimental Setup Task and Benchmark. We evaluate HCDR3 design on RAbD ( Adolf-Bryfogle et al., 2018 ) , peptide design on LNR ( Tsaban et al., 2022 ) , and small-molecule design on CrossDocked2020 ( Francoeur et al., 2020 ) . The fixed evaluation sets contain 60 RAbD targets, 93 LNR targets, and a 100-target subset of CrossDocked2020, respectively. Baselines. We compare against AnewOmni ( Kong et al., 2026 ) , LLM4GEN ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , EnzyAdapter ( Song et al., 2025 ) , and IP-Adapter ( Ye et al., 2023 ) . AnewOmni uses its original pretrained checkpoint without additional training. LLM4GEN and EnzyAdapter adapt the respective representation-fusion mechanisms to the AnewOmni backbone. LLM4GEN applies a single cross-attention module to update native conditioning before the unchanged denoiser. EnzyAdapter uses layerwise cross-attention, concatenation, and projection modules. IP-Adapter applies decoupled cross-attention at each EPT layer, using native queries to attend separately to projected PairFormer single representations. The donor scalar output is added before the shared frozen output projection. All fusion baselines are trained on the common biomolecular task. All trained representation-fusion methods are matched in trainable parameter count (approximately 4.03 million, with a maximum relative difference below 0.1%), with details reported in Table 5 . Evaluation. Following AnewOmni ( Kong et al., 2026 ) , we evaluate structural accuracy and amino-acid recovery for antibody and peptide design. We additionally assess interface quality through local-interface adaptations of DockQ and native-contact recall ( Basu and Wallner, 2016 ) , together with a backbone interface score based on lDDT ( Mariani et al., 2013 ) . Native metrics pool finite candidate scores within each run, whereas interface and supplementary structural metrics first average finite candidates within each target and then weight targets equally. We select one checkpoint per trained run by minimizing the combined native validation loss on a 614-record validation set, weighting each modality by its number of generated blocks. The selected checkpoint is shared across all three modalities. Metric definitions and evaluation procedures are provided in Section D.5 . PairFuse integrates pretrained PairFormer single and pair representations into the evolving invariant block features and native geometric attention of a geometric latent diffusion model, while keeping both pretrained models frozen. Theoretically, we prove that PairFuse preserves rotational equivariance and characterize the additional expressivity of pairwise attention fusion under a stated rank condition ( Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 ). Experimentally, PairFuse achieves the lowest mean complex RMSD and the highest mean interface-quality scores on antibody and peptide benchmarks. For small-molecule design, it achieves favorable docking and atom-type metrics, with mixed results on other chemical-quality metrics ( Section 4.2 ). A limitation is that unknown generated molecular structures, particularly small-molecule ligands, lack direct PairFormer token correspondences, which may affect representation-transfer effectiveness. Future work will explore representation-fusion mechanisms that better accommodate unknown molecular structures and additional pretrained all-atom models.
